items.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024
items.q: He actually got me to play at the Monterey Jazz Festival with Dizzy Gillespie as a guest soloist with the Machito Orchestra

ctx.x: I think that when I listen — of course pan-Latin music — I’ve had a lot of trouble knowing where I am. And I’ve used this excuse with me that oh this music you really need to have lived when you were a kid. You need to hear it from the time you’re a child to really embrace it. And it’s probably not true.

I think it’s easier if you’ve grown up with it. I mean invariably, or undoubtedly, not invariably — undoubtedly the sound of Latin music was embedded in my DNA. So on some level subconsciously I did grow up with it. I grew up with Mario Bauza and Machito and people like that were constant visitors to my house. And in fact one of my earliest playing experiences was I was a bicycle messenger and I loved being a bike messenger but it’s a hard gig. And one day it was raining and I must have been about 16 or 17. It…

hole, you’re not going to be able to. And so I mean you know it was really interesting to me to rediscover the incredible complexity and subtlety of Latin music that you can’t just play. You’re absolutely correct, that you can’t just pick it up. It’s by osmosis. It’s by listening to it. It’s by understanding it. It’s by learning how to play percussion, the great Puerto Rican valve trombonist Papo Vazquez sat me down and actually had me learn the conga patterns and the timbale patterns and all of that is really…
